title: FTC weighs new duties for platforms carrying impersonation ads
description: Agency seeks evidence about ad tools and impersonation scams. No new platform rule has taken effect.
author: David Chen
body: The Federal Trade Commission is asking whether online platforms should face new obligations when their advertising tools help spread ads that impersonate businesses or government agencies. It has opened an advance notice of proposed rulemaking, not adopted a new rule.

The agency's September 24 notice focuses on ad-optimization services offered by social networks, search engines and digital marketplaces. It seeks evidence about how those tools select audiences and shape the delivery of ads, what platforms do to vet advertisers, and whether changes to the existing Impersonation Rule or a separate rule are warranted. Measures under consideration include advertiser screening, monitoring, removing confirmed scam ads and action against offending advertisers.

The FTC says consumers filed more than one million imposter-scam reports in 2025 and reported nearly $3.5 billion in losses. Those are reported losses, not an estimate of all fraud. The agency also says nearly 30% of consumers who reported losing money to scammers in 2025 said the first contact was on social media. Neither figure by itself proves a platform caused a particular loss.

The public comment deadline will be 60 days after the notice appears in the Federal Register. That publication date, rather than September 24, sets the clock. No new platform duty takes effect from this notice alone.

For people searching online for help with a bill or debt, the distinction between an official service and an ad that copies its name matters. Before providing account information or paying a supposed relief provider, navigate independently to the agency or provider's official site. Financialist's state-by-state debt help guide is a separate starting point for understanding state-specific debt rules; it is not a substitute for checking an offer's identity.

sources.label: FTC September 24 announcement on impersonation-ad rulemaking

title: More Amazon Prime subscribers qualify for automatic refunds under revised FTC settlement
description: A revised settlement expands automatic refunds starting October 1; eligible consumers will not have to file a claim.
author: David Chen
body: The Federal Trade Commission says a revised court order will expand refunds to more consumers under its settlement with Amazon over Prime enrollment and cancellation practices. The maximum total payment to an eligible consumer rises from $51 to $200, though that does not mean everyone will receive $200.

The agency announced September 17 that people who used 11 to 20 Prime benefits during a one-year period, previously outside the initial refund group, will become eligible for automatic payments beginning October 1, 2026. Under the revised order, future payments will not require a consumer to file a claim or complete paperwork. Amazon will distribute them by electronic payment or mailed check, according to the FTC.

The original settlement required up to $1.5 billion for consumer redress and a $1 billion civil penalty. The FTC says Amazon had issued more than $845 million in redress by September 2026. A further payment of up to $149 to some consumers who already received refunds is conditional: it would begin by April 2027 if accepted payments have not reached a required threshold by February 2027. It is not a payment scheduled for every prior recipient.

The FTC says it is not contacting consumers about these Amazon refunds and that nobody from Amazon will ask for money to obtain one. A message demanding a fee or personal information to release a payment is not part of this redress process.

If a refund arrives, Financialist's debt-payoff calculator can help compare applying that money to balances under snowball and avalanche strategies. The tool is optional and does not affect eligibility for the settlement.

sources.label: FTC September 17 announcement on revised Amazon refunds

title: September 28 tax deadline approaches for eligible San Carlos Apache Tribe disaster area taxpayers
description: Eligible taxpayers in the San Carlos Apache Tribe disaster area have a September 28 deadline for many postponed filings and payments.
author: James Park
body: Taxpayers covered by IRS disaster relief for severe storms and flooding in the San Carlos Apache Tribe area face a September 28 deadline for many postponed federal tax filings and payments. The relief is limited to eligible affected taxpayers; it is not a nationwide extension.

According to the IRS, qualifying individuals who live in the covered area and businesses whose principal place of business is there can use the postponement. Others whose records needed to meet a deadline are in the covered area can also qualify. The IRS lists additional categories, including eligible relief workers. The postponed window generally covers specified deadlines originally falling on or after October 10, 2025, and before September 28, 2026.

Estimated income tax payments that originally fell in that window are postponed through September 28. The IRS says affected taxpayers will not be penalized for failing to pay those installments if they pay by that date. Not every form or deposit is covered: the agency lists exceptions for certain information returns and employment and excise tax deposits. Anyone relying on the relief should check the complete IRS notice against their own filing obligation.

Eligible taxpayers in the federally declared disaster area may also choose whether to claim qualifying uncovered casualty losses for the disaster year or the prior year. The IRS says individual taxpayers have until October 15, 2026, to make that election. A casualty-loss claim involves separate eligibility and documentation rules; the postponed filing deadline does not automatically establish a deductible loss.

Financialist's Arizona debt-help guide covers a different topic, state debt rules, for readers managing obligations after the storm. It does not explain eligibility for federal disaster tax relief; use the IRS notice for that decision.

sources.label: IRS disaster tax-relief notice for San Carlos Apache Tribe area

title: Hawaii joins proposed Credit Acceptance auto-loan settlement with debt relief
description: Proposed multistate settlement offers potential cash restitution and debt relief for eligible Credit Acceptance borrowers.
author: James Park
body: Hawaii has joined a proposed multistate settlement with auto lender Credit Acceptance Corporation over allegations involving unaffordable loans and add-on products. The consent judgment still needs court approval in participating states, so the proposed relief should not be described as money already paid to every borrower.

In a September 23 announcement, Hawaii's Office of Consumer Protection said the nationwide settlement could provide up to $60 million in cash restitution and up to $634 million in debt forgiveness, with up to $15 million going to settling attorneys general. Those are nationwide maximums or prospective amounts, not a per-person payout. Hawaii expects eligible borrowers in the state to receive nearly $115,000 in direct payments in total and nearly $830,000 in debt relief in total, some of which the office says may already have been provided.

The state says investigators alleged that Credit Acceptance originated some loans it knew or should have known borrowers could not afford. They also alleged that dealers in its network added vehicle service contracts and guaranteed asset protection products without consumers understanding the purchase or believing the products were required to finance the car. These are allegations resolved by the proposed settlement, not findings in this article.

If approved, the judgment would require new disclosures, monitoring of add-on sales and a process to cancel certain products more easily. For qualifying risky loans made beginning December 2025 that fail quickly, the settlement describes a five-year program beginning November 2, 2026, under which qualifying borrowers would get 95% debt relief and would not face collection suits on those loans. Not every Credit Acceptance borrower qualifies.

The Hawaii office says Credit Acceptance must contact consumers entitled to certain types of relief. Borrowers should verify their eligibility through official channels and not assume that an unsolicited message requesting an upfront fee is legitimate. Financialist's Hawaii debt guide offers background on state debt rules, separate from the settlement's eligibility terms.

sources.label: Hawaii Office of Consumer Protection September 23 announcement

title: States reach $2.3 million Labcorp settlement over debt collector's data breach
description: Forty-four states reached an agreement with Labcorp over patient data held by a medical debt collector.
author: David Chen
body: A coalition of 44 state attorneys general has reached an approximately $2.3 million settlement with Labcorp over a 2019 data breach at a medical debt collector that handled Labcorp patient information. The agreement focuses on how the laboratory company oversees vendors holding sensitive patient data; the state announcement does not describe this $2.3 million as a consumer refund fund.

Delaware Attorney General Kathy Jennings announced the settlement September 24. The debt collector was Retrieval-Masters Creditors Bureau, doing business as American Medical Collection Agency, or AMCA. The breach potentially exposed information about more than 27.5 million people nationwide, including 10.2 million Labcorp patients, according to the Delaware announcement. "Potentially exposed" does not mean every person's data was misused.

Under the agreement described by Delaware, Labcorp will strengthen its vendor risk program, maintain an incident-response process for vendor security events, limit sharing of data where appropriate, and impose additional security standards and assessment requirements on debt-collection vendors. A third-party assessor will review its information-security program with a focus on vendor risk management. Labcorp's payment to the states is $2,287,455, including $30,135 to Delaware.

The state distinguishes this multistate agreement from a separate $35 million class-action settlement related to the breach. Consumers should not confuse the two or infer a personal payment from the states' agreement. The Delaware announcement does not set out a claims process for individuals under this state settlement.

Medical bills can reach a collector even when the original provider's name is more familiar to the patient. Anyone contacted about an old medical balance can ask for written details and check the debt independently before providing financial information. Financialist's state debt guides cover general collection rules by location; they do not determine whether someone was affected by this breach.

sources.label: Delaware Department of Justice September 24 announcement

title: FTC tells auto dealers advertised prices must include mandatory fees
description: FTC staff guidance says advertised vehicle prices should include mandatory dealer fees.
author: James Park
body: An automobile's advertised price should be the price a consumer can actually pay to purchase it, excluding only government-required charges, according to price-transparency guidance published by Federal Trade Commission staff. The September 15 FAQs explain the agency's interpretation of existing FTC Act obligations rather than announcing a new loan rate or a blanket cap on dealer fees.

The guidance addresses document fees, rebates, discounts, optional add-ons, negotiations and vehicles still in transit. The central distinction is between a charge a buyer may decline and one the dealer requires to complete the sale. A mandatory dealer fee omitted from an advertised price can make the ad misleading even when the fee eventually appears in paperwork.

The FTC says it previously wrote to 97 auto groups urging dealers to review advertisements and warns it continues to sue dealers accused of advertising one price and charging a higher one through undisclosed fees. Consumers can report a suspected violation to ReportFraud.ftc.gov and should include the dealership and details of the discrepancy, the agency says.

The price of the car and the cost of financing it are related but distinct. A buyer comparing offers should request an itemized out-the-door price and review the amount financed, annual percentage rate, loan length and any add-ons before signing. A longer loan can reduce a monthly payment while raising the overall amount paid. Financialist's debt-payoff calculator can help model a balance repayment strategy, but does not calculate an auto loan's total financing cost.
